analysis.one_liner: Directs the government to negotiate the lowest possible prescription drug prices for Medicare and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to bargain with drug companies for the lowest prices on medicines covered by Medicare's drug benefit — the same bargaining power the Veterans Affairs Department already uses to buy drugs in bulk. It also would have tightened the Medicaid 'best price' rule so discounts given to federal agencies counted when states calculate what drug makers owe them, and let states join together in pools to demand bigger rebates from manufacturers. It was introduced in May 2005, referred to two committees and their health subcommittees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and Medicaid programs, who would pay lower prices for prescription drugs if the federal government used its enormous purchasing power the way the VA does. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicaid and Medicare help pay drug bills.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the 'noninterference' clause in Medicare Part D — the provision that bars the government from interfering with private plans' drug price negotiations — and instead requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the lowest possible prices, using authority similar to the VA's bulk-purchasing power.
It amends Medicaid's 'best price' rule so that the low prices drug makers charge certain federal agencies are counted, rather than excluded, when calculating manufacturer rebates owed to states.
It clarifies that states can form pools to negotiate rebates together, giving smaller states the combined leverage of larger buyers.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a single government buyer negotiating prices down and broader Medicaid rebate obligations, with some risk of lower industry revenue.

drawbacks.text: Critics of government price negotiation argue that a single federal buyer bargaining hard can suppress prices in ways that reduce manufacturers' incentive to develop new medicines, potentially slowing the arrival of future drugs.

Extending the Medicaid 'best price' rule to count federal-agency prices, as the bill does, can make manufacturers reluctant to offer deep discounts anywhere, since one low price raises rebate obligations in every state's Medicaid program.

The bill required the Secretary to both 'have and exercise' negotiating authority, which could have disrupted the existing Part D structure of private plans and their negotiated pharmacy networks in its first years of operation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings for beneficiaries and taxpayers were substantial — the VA's bulk purchasing had long demonstrated that large buyers get lower prices. The tradeoffs are real but manageable: negotiation reduces manufacturer revenue on existing drugs, and the best-price change could create side effects in Medicaid. On balance, letting Medicare negotiate is a change many other federal buyers already use.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dutch Ruppersberger introduced the Prescription Drug Price Fairness Act on May 5, 2005, with no cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee.
Within three weeks, both committees referred it to their Subcommittee on Health — the Energy and Commerce subcommittee on May 12 and the Ways and Means subcommittee on May 23.
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and the private plans and intermediaries that run the Medicare drug benefit kept their negotiating role, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D plans

for.name: Rep. C. A. Dutch Ruppersberger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require HHS to negotiate Medicare drug prices and to tighten Medicaid rebates.

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicare drug benefit provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Health, where it was never considered.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Health, where it was never considered.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors and no votes, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have forced drug makers to accept government-negotiated prices for Medicare drugs and broader Medicaid rebate obligations, cutting revenue on the largest public drug-purchasing programs. Their prices are what beneficiaries and taxpayers pay.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Medicare Part D was built around private plans that negotiate drug prices on the government's behalf; the bill would have shifted that bargaining to the Secretary of HHS, shrinking the plans' and their pharmacy benefit intermediaries' role. They profit from standing between beneficiaries and drug prices.
Counting federal-agency prices in the best-price calculation and allowing state pooling would have increased rebates states collect from manufacturers, lowering state and taxpayer drug costs.
